finding: Test 1 may not be the worst case for spacecraft fires, and its adequacy at lunar or Martian gravity is unknown.
quote: There is compelling evidence that the Test 1 may not be the worst case for spacecraft fires, and we don't have enough information to assess if it is adequate at Lunar or Martian gravity levels.

finding: A cellulose fuel with a 16.5% O2 limiting oxygen index on Earth sustains flames at 14% O2 under spacecraft-like ventilation in microgravity.
quote: the LOI, or limiting oxygen index on Earth in opposed flow is 16.5% O2. However, if the flow is on the order of spacecraft ventilation (5-20 cm/s), flames can be sustained even at 14 % O2.

finding: At spacecraft ventilation speeds (5-20 cm/s) in microgravity, upstream (opposed-flow) flame spread was the only viable flame.
quote: Over most of the range of air ventilation rates (5-20 cm/s) comparable to spacecraft ventilation, upstream flame spread was the only viable flame.

finding: At lunar and Martian gravity, buoyant flows above 20 cm/s make concurrent (Test 1-style) flame spread viable alongside opposed-flow spread.
quote: On the Moon or Mars (0.17g and 0.38 g, respectively), where buoyant flows will be greater than 20 cm/s, the concurrent flame spread will be viable simultaneously with any opposed flow flame.

finding: KC-135 parabolic-flight experiments showed concurrent flames burn faster in partial gravity environments.
quote: Experiments conducted aboard the KC-135 [9] demonstrate the faster burning of concurrent flames in partial gravity environments.

finding: Even a very slight airflow, a fraction of a cm/s, is enough for a low-gravity flame to survive after ventilation is cut.
quote: However, experiments have shown that even a very slight air flow of a fraction of a cm/s [4] is sufficient to allow the flame to survive.

finding: Under very weak ventilation, small non-luminous fingering flames can be almost undetectable yet persist for many minutes.
quote: These flames can become almost undetectable (small, non-luminous) and yet persist for many minutes [10, 11] for a fingering flame spread observed under very weak ventilation.

finding: Raising the flow 100-fold to 50 cm/s did not blow out a tiny fingering flame; it flared into a much larger spreading flame.
quote: When the flow was turned up 100-fold to 50 cm/s, the flame did not blow out as one would expect, but flared up into a much larger spreading flame.

finding: In a 1-g low-stretch analogue, PMMA ignition delay fell threefold, so standard cone tests significantly underestimate microgravity ignition risk.
quote: For a fixed radiant flux, ignition delay times for characterization material PMMA are shown to decrease by a factor of three at low stretch, demonstrating that ignition delay times determined from normal cone tests significantly underestimate the risk in microgravity.

finding: NASA-STD-6001 Test 2 (standard cone) is not conservative: its buoyant flow is much stronger than in low-gravity fires.
quote: These results also demonstrate that current NASA STD 6001 Test 2 (standard cone) is not conservative since it evaluates materials flammability with a much higher inherent buoyant convective flow.

finding: At low stretch, as in low-gravity flows, less convective cooling lowers the critical heat flux needed for ignition.
quote: The critical heat flux for ignition is found to be lowered at low stretch as the convective cooling is reduced.

finding: Some materials that will not burn in 1 g will burn at lunar gravity, or in 0 g with a low-speed flow.
quote: Theoretical and experimental results have demonstrated that some materials that will not burn in 1-g will burn in 0-g (with a low-speed flow) or in partial gravity (such as Lunar-g).

finding: Flame spread rate peaks near lunar gravity, so early numerical and experimental evidence suggested the Moon could be more hazardous.
quote: Early numerical and experimental evidence suggested that Lunar gravity could be more hazardous, since flame spread rate as a function of gravity peaks there [2].

finding: The minimum oxygen concentration needed for flammability is lowest near lunar gravity.
quote: Related work suggests that oxygen concentration for flammability reaches a minimum value in the vicinity of g = g Lunar.

finding: Numerical and experimental evidence suggests lunar gravity is nearly the most flammable gravity condition.
quote: Numerical and experimental evidence suggests that Lunar gravity is nearly the most flammable condition.

finding: KC-135 experiments found downward flame spread rate peaks at partial gravity.
quote: Downward flame spread rate peaks in partial-g [right, Sacksteder; KC-135 experiments].

finding: Keeping O2 partial pressure up in a low-pressure cabin means raising O2 concentration, which makes materials more flammable.
quote: A consequence of raising O2 concentration to sustain O2 partial pressure in a low-pressure environment is that the flammability of materials increases with increasing O2 concentration.

finding: Fewer materials qualify in higher-O2 cabins, a significant challenge for spacecraft design and operations.
quote: The reduction in the number of candidate materials that can be used in higher O2 environments represents a significant challenge in designing and operating a spacecraft.

finding: NASA has limited material flammability data above 30% O2.
quote: However, NASA has limited material flammability data at O2 concentration higher than 30% (F-12a).

finding: Recent testing found very few textiles can pass NASA-STD-6001 Test 1 at 37% O2 and 8.2 psia.
quote: Overall, recent testing revealed very few textiles capable of passing NASA-STD-6001 Test 1, the standard NASA test for flammability, at 37% O2 and 8.2 psia

label: NASA-STD-6001 Test 1
text: Test 1 fails a material that burns more than 12 inches from a standard igniter.
quote: Its simple pass-fail criteria eliminates materials that burn for more than 12 inches from a standardized ignition source.

label: Screened at 1 g
text: Test 1 runs in Earth gravity and assumes a material that passes is safe for spaceflight.
quote: The test is conducted in normal Earth gravity, with the assumption that if a material passes the 1-g test, then it is considered safe for spaceflight.

label: Olson 2004
text: Test 1 may not be the worst case for spacecraft fires; its adequacy at lunar or Martian gravity is unknown.
quote: There is compelling evidence that the Test 1 may not be the worst case for spacecraft fires, and we don't have enough information to assess if it is adequate at Lunar or Martian gravity levels.

label: Passes at 1 g, burns elsewhere
text: Some materials that won't burn in 1 g will burn in 0 g with low flow, or at lunar gravity.
quote: Theoretical and experimental results have demonstrated that some materials that will not burn in 1-g will burn in 0-g (with a low-speed flow) or in partial gravity (such as Lunar-g).

label: Minimum near lunar g
text: The oxygen needed for flammability reaches a minimum near lunar gravity.
quote: Related work suggests that oxygen concentration for flammability reaches a minimum value in the vicinity of g = g Lunar.

label: Blowoff branch (high flow)
text: With strong buoyant flow, air can enter a flame faster than its chemistry can keep pace.
quote: The speed of the air entering the flame can be so high, however, that the chemical reactions are unable to keep pace.

label: Quenching branch (low flow)
text: With too little flow, a flame starves of fresh oxygen and cannot survive indefinitely.
quote: As demonstrated by the data above, the flame cannot survive indefinitely without a supply of fresh oxygen.

label: Why the Moon can be worse
text: At lunar gravity buoyant oxygen supply persists but slows, so a material marginal on Earth may burn.
quote: The same material may be flammable at a lower gravity level (for example, on the Moon) since the crucial mechanism of buoyant oxygen entrainment at the flame base is still present, but at a slower rate

label: Nearly the most flammable
text: Lunar gravity is nearly the most flammable condition, per numerical and experimental evidence.
quote: Numerical and experimental evidence suggests that Lunar gravity is nearly the most flammable condition.

label: Habitat fires at partial g
text: Partial-g habitat fires are expected to be substantially worse than at 0 g and possibly worse than at 1 g.
quote: Consequently, partial-g fire in an extraterrestrial habitat is a real hazard that is expected to be substantially worse than in 0-g and potentially worse than even 1-g.

label: FM2
text: FM2 will burn four solid fuel samples in real, long-duration lunar gravity.
quote: Flammability of Materials on the Moon (FM2) will burn a total of four solid fuel samples in quiescent habitable atmospheres in actual long duration Lunar gravity (Fig. 1).

label: FM2 launch
text: The first combustion experiments on another world are planned to launch in late 2026.
quote: The first-ever combustion experiments on another world will be performed, with a planned launch date of late 2026.

label: FM2 goal
text: FM2 results will bridge NASA's 1-g screening test and real behaviour in reduced gravity.
quote: The results will provide a bridge between the current 1-g material screening method and actual behavior in reduced gravity.

label: Drop towers & aircraft
text: Drop towers (5 s) and aircraft (~25 s) give too little time for significant flame development.
quote: Partial gravity tests can be performed in drop towers [8] and aboard aircraft [2], but the available times are too short to provide significant flame development (5 s for drop tower and ~25 s for aircraft).

label: Rotating sounding rocket
text: A spinning sounding rocket simulated lunar gravity for about 150 s, with Coriolis uncertainty.
quote: A sounding rocket utilizing vehicle rotation to simulate Lunar gravity provided test times on the order of 150 s, burning two different materials, but again the Coriolis force introduces uncertainty.

label: Exploration Atmosphere
text: The lunar-habitat Exploration Atmosphere was revised to 8.2 psia and 34% O2.
quote: Current plans for M2M habitats on the Lunar surface require EVA, thus EA recommendation became 8 psia and 32% O2 but was revised to 8.2 psia and 34% O2 to decrease hypoxia exposure.

label: The trade-off
text: The Exploration Atmosphere eases EVAs but makes fire management harder in higher-than-normal O2.
quote: Unfortunately, the benefits of EA in support of safe and efficient EVAs comes with the challenge of fire management in a higher-than-normal O2% environment.

label: NESC assessment
text: Raising O2 concentration at low cabin pressure increases material flammability.
quote: A consequence of raising O2 concentration to sustain O2 partial pressure in a low-pressure environment is that the flammability of materials increases with increasing O2 concentration.

label: HEO-DM-1006
text: Exploration missions with frequent EVA need 8.2 psia cabins with at least 33.7% O2.
quote: HEO-DM-1006 [ref. 15] specifies that a nominal total cabin pressure of 8.2 psia and O2 greater than or equal to 33.7% is needed for Exploration missions with high-frequency EVA.

label: Lander, habitat, rover
text: The lander, lunar habitat and pressurized rover will nominally run 8.2 psia and 34% O2.
quote: HLS, Lunar habitat and pressurized rover will nominally use 8.2 psia / 34% O2, 66% N2

label: Moon base atmosphere
text: Moon base and rover atmospheres will likely be at least 30% O2 at 10.2 psi or less.
quote: The intermediate oxygen concentration used on the Moon will likely be 30% or greater, with a corresponding pressure of 10.2 psi or less.

label: +40% oxygen
text: That is over 40% more oxygen than Earth's air, making materials much more flammable.
quote: Compared to Earth's atmosphere, that's more than a 40% increase in the oxygen concentration making materials much more flammable.

label: Data gap above 30% O2
text: NASA has limited material flammability data above 30% O2.
quote: However, NASA has limited material flammability data at O2 concentration higher than 30% (F-12a).

label: Max O2 36-40%
text: With control bands and sensor accuracy, habitat O2 could peak at 36-40%.
quote: When provision is made for O2 concentration control bands and sensor accuracy, the maximum O2 concentration could be between 36 and 40%, but the exact numbers will depend on specific vehicle design and hardware capability.

label: Control band
text: Cabin O2 control bands are expected to allow up to 37%.
quote: Control bands are expected to allow up to 37% O2

label: 37% O2 certification
text: Textiles are being certified for 34% O2 plus a 3% margin: a 37% O2 target.
quote: Now, the agency focus is on certifying textiles for use in 34% O2 plus a 3% margin, resulting in a target of 37% O2.

label: CFI-G
text: ACME's CFI-G ran the highest-oxygen microgravity tests in PSI.
quote: Microgravity tests with the highest oxygen concentrations were conducted as part of the ACME's Cool Flames Investigation with Gases (CFI-G).

label: Up to 85% O2
text: CFI-G flowed up to 85% oxygen from a spherical burner, making an inside-out flame.
quote: an oxygen-nitrogen mixture of up to 85% oxygen flowed from the spherical burner creating an inside-out flame.

label: Challenge brief
text: PSI currently holds no partial-gravity combustion data.
quote: there is currently no partial-gravity combustion data available in PSI.

label: LUCI & FM2
text: Partial-gravity data are expected from LUCI and FM2.
quote: We expect such data will be added in the future, for example from the Lunar-g Combustion Investigation (LUCI) and the Flammability of Materials on the Moon (FM2) experiment.

label: E-FIELD mimicry
text: ACME's E-FIELD Flames mimicked partial gravity by acting on flame ions with an electric field.
quote: Partial gravity was mimicked in ACME's Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames (E-FIELD Flames) experiment through the effect of the electric field on the ions that naturally occur in flames.

label: The naive bound
text: The brief suggests 0-g and 1-g results could bound behaviour at intermediate gravity.
quote: Microgravity and normal-gravity results could bound what occurs at intermediate gravity levels.

label: Detection in PSI
text: Fire detection was tested in microgravity by SAME and SAME-R.
quote: Fire detection was tested in microgravity through the Smoke and Aerosol Measurement Experiment studies (SAME and SAME-R).

label: Apollo 1 (1967)
text: In Apollo 1's pure-oxygen cabin the fire spread quickly and ruptured the Command Module pressure vessel.
quote: Because of the pure oxygen atmosphere, the fire spread quickly, causing a rapid rise in temperature and pressure that led to the rupture of the Command Module pressure vessel.

label: Apollo 13 (1970)
text: An oxygen tank blew up in flight, and the second oxygen tank then failed.
quote: oxygen tank number two blew up, leading to the subsequent failure of tank number one.

label: Mir (1997)
text: A fire in an oxygen-generating system endangered all six crew aboard Mir.
quote: On Feb. 24, 1997, the six crew members aboard the Russian space station Mir faced significant danger when a fire ignited in an oxygen generating system.
